questions.question: Using the chapter's definitions, which of these purchases counts as a need?
options: Safety boots that a new construction job requires
A newer phone model while the current one still works
A premium streaming plan with extra channels added
A second pair of boots in a fashionable new style
questions.correctAnswer: Safety boots that a new construction job requires
questions.explanation: Wants are things that are not necessary for living, income, or protecting what you have. Boots that a job requires are necessary for income, so they are a need. The other three are upgrades.

source.quote: Wants are upgrades and other things that would be nice to have but are not necessary for living, income, or protecting what you have.

questions.question: In the classroom exercise, why do students pick their wants at the very end?
options: Wants are bad, so students should avoid buying them
Housing prices depend on which wants students choose
Wants get only the money left after required costs
Wants repeat every month, so they form the floor
questions.correctAnswer: Wants get only the money left after required costs
questions.explanation: The order is the lesson. Things you must pay come off the top, and wants are chosen from whatever is left in the budget.

source.quote: Only then do they choose which wants to pay for, based on how much is left in their budget. The order is the lesson.

questions.question: Why can the bathtub picture mislead someone whose month balances on paper, and what kind of budget addresses the problem?
questions.explanation: Money comes in and goes out at different times. The tub can empty mid-month even if the whole month balances, so a cash flow budget tracks timing week to week.

source.quote: The picture breaks on timing, because a real paycheck arrives in lumps on set days while many bills leave on other days

rubric.point: Income arrives in lumps on set days, while bills leave on other days.
rubric.quote: a real paycheck arrives in lumps on set days while many bills leave on other days

rubric.point: So you can run out mid-month even if the month as a whole balances.
rubric.quote: so the tub can run dry mid-month even when the month as a whole balances

rubric.point: A cash flow budget tracks timing to make sure there is enough each week.
rubric.quote: A cash flow budget is all about tracking the timing of your income and expenses to make sure you have enough from week to week.

questions.modelAnswer: The bathtub treats the month as one total, but paychecks arrive on set days and bills leave on other days, so you can run dry mid-month even when the month balances. A cash flow budget fixes this by tracking timing week to week.

questions.question: Dana sees a half-price coupon for a gaming console she had not planned for. What does the chapter's advice suggest she do?
options: Buy it, since the discount saves her money overall
Buy it only if the coupon expires later this week
Buy it, but cut her grocery bill to cover the cost
Skip it, because it is not in her spending plan
questions.correctAnswer: Skip it, because it is not in her spending plan
questions.explanation: A bargain on a want is still spending on a want. The plan, not the price tag, decides what to buy.

source.quote: The same guide warns not to let a sale or discount coupon persuade you to buy something you do not really need and that is not in your spending plan.

questions.question: After a month of tracking, how does marking the items that repeat every month help you decide where to cut?
questions.explanation: Repeating items tend to be needs and obligations that set the floor of the month. The other items are mostly wants, which is where cuts can be made.

source.quote: Circle the items that are the same every month, like rent, car, or phone payments. These are often your needs and obligations.

rubric.point: Repeating items such as rent or phone payments are usually needs and obligations.
rubric.quote: Circle the items that are the same every month, like rent, car, or phone payments. These are often your needs and obligations.

rubric.point: The things you can eliminate or cut back on are generally wants.
rubric.quote: Then look for areas you can eliminate or cut back on, and these will generally be wants.

rubric.point: The repeating items show the floor of the month, and the rest is where your choices are.
rubric.quote: The repeating items show you the floor of your month. The rest is where your choices live.

questions.modelAnswer: The items that repeat every month, like rent or phone payments, are usually needs that set the floor of your month. Everything else is mostly wants, so that is where you look for things to cut.

sets.title: Chapter 2: A cushion for bad days

questions.question: According to the chapter, how should a person think about a surprise bill, given the 2025 survey results?
options: As a problem that only affects households with low incomes
As a cost that a careful budget will already have listed
As an ordinary event that most adults meet in a typical year
As rare bad luck that mostly happens to other households
questions.correctAnswer: As an ordinary event that most adults meet in a typical year
questions.explanation: The survey found that 59 percent of adults had an unexpected expense in the prior year. The chapter concludes that surprise bills are normal, not someone else's bad luck.

source.quote: Those numbers change how a surprise bill should be read. It is not bad luck that happens to someone else. In a normal year, more than half of adults meet one.

questions.question: In what way is emergency money unlike a real cushion you fall onto?
options: It stays the same size no matter how often it is used
It shrinks each time it is used until you fill it again
It only protects you from large shocks like losing a job
It cannot catch a fall unless it is kept in cash at home
questions.correctAnswer: It shrinks each time it is used until you fill it again
questions.explanation: The chapter says the picture breaks because a real cushion keeps its size, while emergency money gets thinner each time it pays a bill until it is refilled.

source.quote: a real cushion stays the same size after you fall on it, but this one gets thinner every time it catches you, until you fill it back up.

questions.question: Why can the same surprise bill end up costing more for a household with no cushion than for one with a cushion?
questions.explanation: Without savings, the household has to borrow, and borrowing adds a cost on top of the bill. A cushion pays the bill at its original size.

source.quote: If a surprise is paid by borrowing, the one-time emergency expense may grow significantly larger than the original bill.

rubric.point: Without a cushion, the household often has to borrow to pay the bill.
rubric.quote: A small bill becomes a large one when the only way to pay it is to borrow.

rubric.point: Borrowing adds a price on top of the bill, so the total grows.
rubric.quote: That extra cost is the price of borrowing, and a later chapter takes it apart.

rubric.point: A cushion pays the bill at its original size.
rubric.quote: For now, the idea is easy to hold: the cushion pays the bill at its real size.

questions.modelAnswer: Without a cushion, the household usually has to borrow, and the price of borrowing gets added on top, so the bill grows. With a cushion, it pays the bill at its real size.

questions.question: Dana wants a home for her emergency money that is safe, easy to reach, and hard to spend by accident. Which choice best fits the chapter's advice?
options: A separate bank account used only for emergencies
An envelope of cash kept in a drawer at her home
A prepaid card she also uses for weekly groceries
Her everyday checking account, alongside her pay
questions.correctAnswer: A separate bank account used only for emergencies
questions.explanation: A bank account is among the safest places, and keeping it separate from everyday money makes it harder to dip into. Cash at home can be lost or stolen, and mixing the cushion with everyday spending money invites spending it.

source.quote: Many guides suggest a separate account used only for the cushion. Keeping it apart from everyday spending money makes it harder to dip into for things that are not emergencies.

questions.question: What are the two sizes of emergency cushion the chapter describes, and why do most people build the smaller one first?
questions.explanation: The small cushion covers repair bills, and the large one covers months without pay. People start small because it is reachable and because repair bills are the most common shock.

source.quote: Most people build the small one first, because it is reachable and because the repair bill is the shock they meet most often.

rubric.point: The small cushion covers a single surprise such as a repair bill.
rubric.quote: There are two sizes of cushion here, and it helps to keep them apart. The small one catches a repair bill.

rubric.point: The large cushion covers months without income, such as after a job loss.
rubric.quote: The large one carries a household through months without a paycheck.

rubric.point: The small one comes first because it is within reach and matches the most frequent shock.
rubric.quote: Most people build the small one first, because it is reachable and because the repair bill is the shock they meet most often.

rubric.point: A first goal of a few hundred to a thousand dollars covers many common bills.
rubric.quote: Setting aside $500 to $1,000 can cover many unexpected expenses.

questions.modelAnswer: There is a small cushion for surprises like a car repair and a large one for living through months without a paycheck. People build the small one first because it is reachable and repair bills are the shock they meet most often.

sets.title: Chapter 3: Banks, credit unions and deposit insurance

questions.question: According to the chapter, what makes it possible for a bank to pay you interest on your savings?
options: The deposit insurance fund pays interest on every insured balance
It lends depositors' money out and earns more than it pays them
Customers who pull money from CDs early fund everyone else's interest
It keeps each balance in its vault and charges a fee to guard it
questions.correctAnswer: It lends depositors' money out and earns more than it pays them
questions.explanation: Your deposit joins a pool that the bank lends from. The bank earns more from those loans than it pays you, and that difference is what lets it pay interest.

source.quote: Because it lends out the money its depositors leave with it, and it earns more from that lending than it pays you.

questions.question: Jordan has $200,000 in checking and $100,000 in savings, both in his name alone, at one insured bank. If the bank fails, how much of this money is guaranteed?
options: $250,000, one limit for both
$500,000, a limit for each
$200,000, the checking only
$300,000, the full balance
questions.correctAnswer: $250,000, one limit for both
questions.explanation: Both accounts are in the same ownership category at the same bank, so their balances are added together and share a single $250,000 limit.

source.quote: You are insured up to $250,000 for the combined balance of the two, not for each.

questions.question: Sam already has $250,000 in a savings account in his name alone at Bank A. He wants his next $50,000 to be insured as well. Which choice would leave that $50,000 uninsured?
options: Opening a checking account in his name alone at Bank A
Opening a savings account in his name alone at Bank B
Adding it to a joint account with his partner at Bank A
Buying a certificate of deposit in his name at Bank B
questions.correctAnswer: Opening a checking account in his name alone at Bank A
questions.explanation: A second account in his name alone at the same bank falls under the limit he has already used up. A different bank or a joint account would each bring a separate limit.

source.quote: Per bank means a second bank brings a second limit. Per ownership category means accounts you own alone are counted apart from accounts you own jointly with someone else.

questions.question: Robbers take a large amount of cash from your insured bank, but the bank stays open. What happens to your account balance?
options: Nothing, because the bank's own insurance covers its loss
The FDIC repays it, up to $250,000 per ownership category
It is frozen until the government closes the bank down
It shrinks by your share of the cash taken from the pool
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing, because the bank's own insurance covers its loss
questions.explanation: A robbery costs the bank money, not its customers, because the bank carries its own insurance. Deposit insurance only applies when a bank fails, meaning the government has closed it.

source.quote: A fire or a bank robbery may cost the bank money, but it should not cost the bank's customers. The bank carries its own insurance for that.

questions.question: The chapter tells you to check a credit union's insurance before trusting it with your cushion. What is the risk it is warning about?
options: Credit unions lend out deposits, while banks keep them in vaults
Its coverage may not be backed by the United States government
Members must apply for federal coverage before they are protected
Federal credit union insurance has a lower limit than a bank's
questions.correctAnswer: Its coverage may not be backed by the United States government
questions.explanation: Some state-chartered credit unions use private insurers, and that coverage lacks federal backing. Federal credit union insurance has the same $250,000 limit as a bank and comes automatically when you join.

source.quote: Some state-chartered credit unions are insured by private companies instead, and that coverage is not backed by the United States government.

sets.title: Chapter 4: Credit, debt and your credit report

questions.question: Dev is choosing between two credit cards. Card A has a lower interest rate but adds extra fees. Card B has a slightly higher rate and no other charges. Which figure should he compare to see the yearly cost of borrowing on each card?
options: Each card's minimum payment
Each card's interest rate alone
Each card's APR
Each card's daily periodic rate
questions.correctAnswer: Each card's APR
questions.explanation: The APR combines the interest rate with the card's other charges into one yearly figure. That makes it the fair number to compare when fees differ between cards.

source.quote: Card companies add the interest rate and the card's other charges together into that one figure. The APR is the cost of borrowing money over a year.

questions.question: Jordan's card has no grace period. He could pay $300 toward his balance on the 5th of the month or wait until the due date on the 25th. Why would paying on the 5th cost him less?
options: Interest is figured each day on his balance, so fewer unpaid days means less interest
Interest is charged only on whatever balance is still left on the due date itself
Early payments are always applied first to the balance with the lowest interest rate
Paying early lets him skip the minimum payment that would otherwise be due next month
questions.correctAnswer: Interest is figured each day on his balance, so fewer unpaid days means less interest
questions.explanation: Many cards work out interest every day from the average daily balance. Lowering the balance sooner cuts the interest charged on the days that follow.

source.quote: Without a grace period, timing still matters. Because interest builds up day by day, paying some or all of the balance sooner means paying less interest.

questions.question: Lena's card has a grace period. In March she charges $400 in purchases and pays the full $400 by the due date. What interest does she owe on those purchases?
options: One month of interest figured at the card's APR
Interest for each day the $400 went unpaid in March
None, since the full balance was paid by the due date
Only the daily periodic rate for a single day
questions.correctAnswer: None, since the full balance was paid by the due date
questions.explanation: With a grace period, paying the whole balance by the due date avoids interest on purchases entirely.

source.quote: If your card has a grace period, paying the whole balance by the due date each month avoids interest on purchases.

questions.question: Why can a modest card purchase turn into years of bills when someone pays only the minimum, and how does paying more change that?
questions.explanation: Interest keeps being added to the balance each month, so small payments barely shrink the debt. Paying more shortens the time and lowers the total cost.

source.quote: With high balances, it can take years, even decades, to pay a card off that way. Each month, interest is added to what you owe.

rubric.point: Interest is added to the balance every month, so the debt keeps growing back.
rubric.quote: Each month, interest is added to what you owe. That is how a modest purchase becomes a long bill.

rubric.point: Paying more than the minimum means paying the card off sooner and paying less in total.
rubric.quote: A borrower who pays more than the minimum each month pays the card off in less time, and pays less in total.

questions.modelAnswer: Paying only the minimum doesn't clear the debt, and interest is added to what you owe every month, so the balance barely moves for years. Paying more than the minimum gets the card paid off sooner and costs less overall.

questions.question: How could a mistake on your credit report end up costing you money, and what does the chapter suggest doing about it?
questions.explanation: An error can lower your score, and lenders use scores to set rates. Checking your free reports ahead of time lets you fix the error first.

source.quote: Errors on a credit report can lower your score artificially, which could mean a higher interest rate. The fix is to look before you need a loan.

rubric.point: An error can lower your credit score even though your real behavior has not changed.
rubric.quote: Errors on a credit report can lower your score artificially, which could mean a higher interest rate.

rubric.point: Lenders use scores to decide the interest rate you get, so a lower score can mean a higher rate.
rubric.quote: Lenders also use scores to help decide the interest rate and credit limit you receive.

rubric.point: Check the free report from each company every year, well before you need a loan, because each report can differ.
rubric.quote: You can get a free report from each nationwide credit reporting company once every 12 months, and each report can hold different information.

questions.modelAnswer: An error can drag your score down, and lenders use your score to set your interest rate, so you could be charged more. The fix is to pull your free report from each company every year, well before you need a loan, so you have time to correct mistakes.

questions.question: Under simple interest at an assumed 5% a year, why does a $1,000 deposit gain the same dollar amount every year?
options: Interest is figured only on the original deposit, which never changes
The rate is lowered a little each year to keep the gain level
The bank caps the yearly interest at one fixed dollar amount
Each year's interest is added to the base used for the next year
questions.correctAnswer: Interest is figured only on the original deposit, which never changes
questions.explanation: Simple interest is paid only on the principal. Because that base stays the same, each year adds the same amount. Adding interest to the base is what compound interest does.

source.quote: Each year adds the same amount, because the base never changes.

questions.question: At an assumed 5%, $1,000 grows to nearly the same total under simple and compound interest after 10 years, but the totals are far apart after 30 years. What does the chapter conclude from this?
options: Simple interest catches up again if the money is left even longer
Later years add the most growth, so extra time matters a great deal
The interest rate matters more than the number of years invested
Compound interest only starts to work after the first ten years
questions.correctAnswer: Later years add the most growth, so extra time matters a great deal
questions.explanation: The gap between the two kinds of interest is small early and grows large at the end. The chapter says this is why time matters so much, because the last decade does more work than the first.

source.quote: The early years look almost the same, and the difference piles up at the end. That is why time matters so much: the last decade does more work than the first.

questions.question: A saver compares an assumed 5% yearly return with an assumed 7% yearly return, both compounded yearly. About how many years sooner does the money double at the higher rate?
options: About 10 years sooner
About 2 years sooner
About 13 years sooner
About 4 years sooner
questions.correctAnswer: About 4 years sooner
questions.explanation: Money doubles in about 14.2 years at 5% and in about 10.2 years at 7%, a difference of about 4 years. This shows that a few points of rate change the answer by years.

source.quote: At an assumed 5% it doubles in about 14.2 years. At an assumed 7% it doubles in about 10.2 years.

questions.question: In the SEC's 1929 example, why did people who kept putting money into the market through the 1930s do better than people who put everything in at the 1929 peak, and what rule does the chapter draw from it?
questions.explanation: The lump-sum investors bought at the top and had to wait decades to get back to even. The steady investors kept buying while prices were low. The lesson is that steady saving over time matters more than choosing a start date.

source.quote: Those who kept adding money through the 1930s "would have done very well for themselves", because prices were lower then.

rubric.point: Those who invested everything at the peak waited over 20 years just to get back to the same level.
rubric.quote: people who put all their money into the market at its 1929 peak, before the crash, waited over 20 years for it to return to the same level.

rubric.point: Those who kept adding money bought at the lower prices of the 1930s.
rubric.quote: Those who kept adding money through the 1930s "would have done very well for themselves", because prices were lower then.

rubric.point: The rule is that consistent saving over a long time beats trying to pick the right moment.
rubric.quote: Steady saving matters more than a clever start date. Time in beats timing.

questions.modelAnswer: The people who put everything in at the 1929 peak bought at the top and waited over 20 years to get back to even, while the steady adders kept buying at the lower prices of the 1930s. The rule is that consistent saving over a long time matters more than picking the perfect start date.

questions.question: In the example of saving $100 a month for 30 years, what does the split of the final total show about how compound growth works?
questions.explanation: Most of the $83,226 is not money the saver deposited. It comes from interest earning more interest over 30 years.

source.quote: Of that, $36,000 is the deposits themselves and $47,226 is growth. More than half the final pile is money the saver never put in.

rubric.point: The saver ends with $83,226 after 30 years of $100 monthly deposits.
rubric.quote: Adding $100 every month for 30 years, at an assumed 5% compounded monthly, builds $83,226.

rubric.point: Only $36,000 is deposits; the larger part, $47,226, is growth the saver never put in.
rubric.quote: More than half the final pile is money the saver never put in.

rubric.point: This happens because earned interest joins the pile and then earns interest itself.
rubric.quote: Interest from last year joins the pile, and this year it earns interest too.

questions.modelAnswer: Of the $83,226, only $36,000 is the saver's own deposits, and the other $47,226 is growth. Because interest keeps earning interest, more than half the final total is money the saver never put in.

sets.title: Chapter 6: Stocks, bonds and funds: what an index fund and an ETF are

questions.question: A company goes bankrupt. Ana holds its bonds, Ben holds its preferred stock, and Cara holds its common stock. Who is paid first?
options: Cara, the common stockholder
All three are paid at once
Ben, the preferred stockholder
Ana, the bondholder
questions.correctAnswer: Ana, the bondholder
questions.explanation: In a bankruptcy, bondholders are paid before anyone else. Preferred stockholders come next, and common stockholders get whatever is left.

source.quote: When a company goes bankrupt, its bondholders are paid first and holders of preferred stock next. A common stockholder gets whatever is left, which may be nothing.

questions.question: An investor needs cash and sells her bond three years before it comes due. What can she expect to receive for it?
options: Exactly the full principal she originally lent
An amount that may be above or below its face value
Only the interest the bond has paid so far
The face value plus all the remaining interest
questions.correctAnswer: An amount that may be above or below its face value
questions.explanation: The full principal is only guaranteed back if the bond is held until it comes due. Sold early, its price can be higher or lower than face value.

source.quote: Sold before it comes due, a bond may be worth more or less than its face value.

questions.question: An investor places an order for mutual fund shares at 11 a.m. on a weekday. What price will she pay per share?
options: The net asset value from the previous day
The exchange price at the moment of her order
The next net asset value the fund calculates
Whatever price another investor will accept
questions.correctAnswer: The next net asset value the fund calculates
questions.explanation: Mutual fund shares are bought from the fund itself at the next calculated NAV. They are not traded on an exchange or with other investors.

source.quote: When the value of a fund's holdings rises, after its costs and debts are taken out, its NAV rises too. A mutual fund share is bought at the next calculated NAV.

questions.question: Why does an index fund usually cost less to hold than an actively managed fund?
options: It trades less because it only follows its index
A government agency insures it, so it carries less risk
It buys its shares in large blocks straight from the fund
Its manager's skill lets it beat the market more often
questions.correctAnswer: It trades less because it only follows its index
questions.explanation: A passive fund just holds what is in its index. That means less trading, lower taxes on gains, and lower costs than active management.

source.quote: Passive management usually means less trading, lower taxes on gains, and lower costs than active management.

questions.question: Two index funds hold the same companies. One gives bigger companies a bigger share, and the other gives every company the same share. Why might their returns differ?
questions.explanation: How an index is weighted decides how much each company's results count toward the whole, so the same companies can produce different returns.

source.quote: Another kind gives every company an equal place, and the two can return very different amounts.

rubric.point: In a size-weighted index, the largest companies make up much more of the fund, so their results dominate.
rubric.quote: In one common kind, the largest companies make up a much larger share of the list than the smallest ones.

rubric.point: In an equal-weighted index, each company counts the same, so small companies matter more and the returns can differ a lot.
rubric.quote: Another kind gives every company an equal place, and the two can return very different amounts.

questions.modelAnswer: In the size-weighted fund, the biggest companies make up most of the fund, so their results drive the return. In the equal-weighted fund, every company counts the same, so if smaller companies do better or worse than the big ones, the two funds can end up with very different returns.

questions.question: A company goes bankrupt and its assets are sold to pay its investors. Which group is paid last?
options: Every investor is paid an equal share
Holders of its preferred stock
Holders of its bonds
Holders of its common stock
questions.correctAnswer: Holders of its common stock
questions.explanation: Bondholders are paid first and preferred stockholders next. Common stockholders get only what is left, which may be nothing.

source.quote: A common stockholder gets whatever is left, and that may be nothing. Owning a share means standing at the back of the line.

questions.question: You own a bond that pays 3% a year. You want to sell it two years before it matures, but new bonds now pay 5%. What is likely to happen?
options: Buyers will pay extra for it because it is older
You may have to sell it below its face value
You will receive exactly its face value at the sale
You are not allowed to sell it until it matures
questions.correctAnswer: You may have to sell it below its face value
questions.explanation: When rates rise, newer bonds pay more. An older bond with a lower rate is less attractive, so you may have to sell it at a discount before maturity.

source.quote: When rates rise, newer bonds pay more, so an older bond with a lower rate may have to be sold at a discount.

questions.question: Why does spreading money across different kinds of assets reduce risk, instead of just averaging out the losses?
questions.explanation: Diversification works because asset classes do not all fall together. The conditions that hurt one asset class can help another.

source.quote: It works because different kinds of assets do not all fall at once. Conditions that make one asset class do poorly may improve returns for another.

rubric.point: Different kinds of assets do not all drop at the same time.
rubric.quote: It works because different kinds of assets do not all fall at once.

rubric.point: The conditions that hurt one asset class may help another.
rubric.quote: Conditions that make one asset class do poorly may improve returns for another.

rubric.point: Gains or steady value in some holdings can make up for losses in others.
rubric.quote: The hope is that if one investment loses money, the others make up for those losses.

questions.modelAnswer: Different kinds of assets do not all fall at once, and the conditions that hurt one can actually help another. So when one investment loses money, others may hold steady or rise and make up for the loss.

questions.question: Your plan was 60% stocks, but market gains have pushed stocks up to 80% of your portfolio. Which action brings the portfolio back to your plan?
options: Buy more stocks while their prices keep rising
Sell some stocks and put the money into bonds
Keep the new mix, since gains have lowered the risk
Sell some bonds and use the money to buy stocks
questions.correctAnswer: Sell some stocks and put the money into bonds
questions.explanation: Rebalancing means cutting back on the group that grew too large and adding to the other asset categories, so the original mix is restored.

source.quote: To get back to your mix, you may need to sell some stocks or add money to other asset categories.

questions.question: Why might a mutual fund investor never receive a bill for the fund's yearly operating costs?
options: A government agency covers the running costs
The seller pays them out of the sales load
The costs are taken out of the fund's assets
Funds charge these costs only when you sell
questions.correctAnswer: The costs are taken out of the fund's assets
questions.explanation: The fund deducts its expenses from its NAV, so investors pay them indirectly without writing a check. The costs are still listed in the prospectus.

source.quote: These costs are taken out of the fund's assets, which lowers your return. Funds deduct fees and expenses from NAV, so you pay them without ever writing a check.

sets.title: Chapter 8: Accounts and taxes: 401(k), IRA and Roth

questions.question: What happens to the income tax on money you put into a traditional 401(k) from your paycheck?
options: It is paid only on the earnings and never on the deposits
It is paid later, when the money comes out in retirement
It is paid now, and the withdrawals later are tax-free
It is cancelled for good as a reward for saving
questions.correctAnswer: It is paid later, when the money comes out in retirement
questions.explanation: The chapter says the 401(k) does not skip the tax. It moves it from the year you earn the money to the year you take it out and spend it.

source.quote: So the tax is not skipped. It is moved, from the year you earn the money to the year you spend it.

questions.question: According to the chapter, why can putting off the tax on retirement savings leave you with more money?
options: Deferred savings are taxed only on deposits, never on their growth
The tax rate on retirement withdrawals is fixed below today's rate
Money not paid in tax now stays invested and earns its own returns
The IRS adds matching money to accounts that delay their taxes
questions.correctAnswer: Money not paid in tax now stays invested and earns its own returns
questions.explanation: The advantage comes from compounding. The amount that would have gone to tax stays in the account and grows for decades. Whether you end up ahead still depends on your future tax rate, which nobody knows for certain.

source.quote: Money that would have gone to tax this year stays in the account instead, and it earns returns of its own for decades.

questions.question: A 52-year-old worker wants to put the most allowed into a 401(k) in 2027. What is the most they can put in?
questions.explanation: For 2027 the base limit is $25,500. Workers aged 50 and older can put in up to $34,000 that year.

source.quote: Workers 50 and older could put in up to $34,000 a year starting in 2027.

questions.question: In 2026, a 40-year-old with plenty of taxable pay puts $5,000 into a traditional IRA and $5,000 into a Roth IRA. What problem has this caused, and how can they fix it?
questions.explanation: Both IRAs count toward a single $7,500 limit, so this person has put in $2,500 too much. The excess is taxed every year it stays in the account.

source.quote: The same combined limit covers every Roth and traditional IRA you own, so opening a second account does not double it.

rubric.point: The $7,500 limit for 2026 covers both IRAs together, so $10,000 is $2,500 over the limit.
rubric.quote: For 2026, the total you put into all of your traditional and Roth IRAs together can be no more than $7,500

rubric.point: The excess is taxed at 6% for every year it stays in the IRA.
rubric.quote: Excess contributions are taxed at 6% per year for each year the extra stays in the IRA.

rubric.point: To fix it, they take the excess and its earnings back out by the due date of their tax return.
rubric.quote: The way out is to take the excess and its earnings back out by your tax return's due date.

questions.modelAnswer: They have gone $2,500 over the 2026 limit, because $7,500 is the total for all their IRAs combined, and that excess is taxed 6% every year it stays in the account. They should take the extra $2,500, plus anything it earned, back out by their tax return's due date.

questions.question: The chapter calls retirement accounts containers. Why does choosing a tax-sheltered account not settle how well your money will grow?
questions.explanation: The account controls only how the money is taxed. Growth depends on the investments held inside it, and those investments' fees still reduce your returns.

source.quote: The account decides how taxes treat the money; the investments inside decide how it grows.

rubric.point: The account itself is not an investment; it holds investments such as stocks, bonds and funds.
rubric.quote: These accounts are not investments themselves. They are containers. A 401(k) or an IRA can hold the stocks, bonds and index funds

rubric.point: The account sets the tax treatment, while the investments inside determine the growth.
rubric.quote: The account decides how taxes treat the money; the investments inside decide how it grows.

rubric.point: Fund fees still reduce returns inside the account, so expense ratios still matter.
rubric.quote: Fees still count inside a tax-sheltered account, so the expense ratio of each fund matters as much here as anywhere.

questions.modelAnswer: The account only decides how the money is taxed. The stocks, bonds or funds you hold inside it decide how it grows, and their fees still eat into your returns, so you still have to pick good, low-cost investments.

questions.question: A neighbor tells you about a fund that he says pays 20 percent a year and cannot lose money. Based on the chapter, how should you treat this pitch?
options: As a good deal worth checking, since high returns usually mean low risk
As safe enough if the neighbor has already made money from the fund
As a sign of a scam, since anyone claiming little or no risk is a scammer
As acceptable if you invest only a small amount at first to test it
questions.correctAnswer: As a sign of a scam, since anyone claiming little or no risk is a scammer
questions.explanation: Every investment carries risk, and high returns come with high risks. The FTC rule in the chapter says that anyone who claims little or no risk is a scammer.

source.quote: The Federal Trade Commission's rule is that anyone who claims an investment has little or no risk, or will pay without much time and effort, is a scammer.

questions.question: Why does a scammer gain so much by telling you an offer will be gone tomorrow?
questions.explanation: The rush removes your time to check the offer, and checking is what protects you. A real offer would still be there later.

source.quote: Notice what the rush does. It takes away the one thing that protects you, which is time to check.

rubric.point: The rush takes away your time to check the offer, which is your main protection.
rubric.quote: It takes away the one thing that protects you, which is time to check.

rubric.point: Pressure such as limited space or a special deal is meant to make you skip research.
rubric.quote: They may say space is limited, or that you are getting a special deal, so that you skip the research.

rubric.point: A real investment can wait. A fake one needs your answer before you ask anyone else.
rubric.quote: A real investment will still be there next week. A fake one needs your answer before you ask anyone else.

questions.modelAnswer: The deadline takes away your time to check the offer, research it, or ask someone else, and that time is what protects you. A real investment would still be there next week, so a fake one has to get your answer fast.

questions.question: You get a text that claims to be from the SEC. It says your account has a problem and gives a link to fix it. What does the chapter say you should do?
options: Reach the agency yourself through its official phone number or website
Call the phone number listed in the text to talk to a real person
Click the link but enter only your name, not your account number
Reply to the text and ask the sender to prove who they are
questions.correctAnswer: Reach the agency yourself through its official phone number or website
questions.explanation: Scammers pose as trusted bodies, even the SEC. The fix is to cut the line and contact the agency through its official number or website, not through anything the message gives you.

source.quote: Contact the bank, company or agency through its official phone number or website, and ask whether there is a real problem.

questions.question: In a slow-building scam, why would a fraudster let you take out a small amount of money before asking for more?
questions.explanation: The small payout looks like proof that the scheme is real. That builds trust, so you will put in larger sums later.

source.quote: The small withdrawal is the hook, and it works because it looks like proof.

rubric.point: The scammer first builds trust, for example by posing as a friend or claiming the contact was an accident.
rubric.quote: Fraudsters may reach out on social media or by text, pretend to be an old friend, or claim they contacted you by accident.

rubric.point: The withdrawal works as a hook because it looks like proof that the profits are real.
rubric.quote: The small withdrawal is the hook, and it works because it looks like proof.

rubric.point: Once you trust it, they ask you to invest larger sums.
rubric.quote: Then they make it look as if you have profited, and may even let you withdraw a small amount. After that they ask you to invest larger sums.

questions.modelAnswer: Getting a little money back makes the scheme look real, so it works like proof and wins your trust. Once you trust it, the scammer asks you to put in much larger sums.

questions.question: In a pump-and-dump scheme involving a new coin, what happens to the people who bought because of the social media hype?
options: They lose most of their money after the promoters sell
They get their money back once the coin is officially registered
They profit as long as they buy before the promoters do
They gain slowly because the price keeps rising after the hype
questions.correctAnswer: They lose most of their money after the promoters sell
questions.explanation: The promoters push the price up, sell before the hype ends, and then the price falls quickly. Everyone else who bought loses most of their money.

source.quote: Then they sell before the hype ends. Then the price falls quickly, and everyone else who bought loses most of their money.

questions.question: Maya has $1,000 saved, a credit card balance charging 18 percent, and no emergency fund. Following the chapter's order, where should her $1,000 go first?
options: Into a diversified index fund with low annual fees
Into savings until six months of income is set aside
Toward paying down the credit card balance
Into a 401(k) to collect the tax break and match
questions.correctAnswer: Toward paying down the credit card balance
questions.explanation: The chapter puts high interest debt as the first stop. No investment can guarantee returns that beat a credit card's rate, so only the money left over moves on.

source.quote: No investment offers guaranteed returns that outweigh the interest on a credit card or other high interest debt. So the sum goes to high interest debt first, and only what is left walks on.

questions.question: According to the chapter, how can one repair bill keep costing money long after it is paid?
options: It goes on a card or loan, where interest and fees keep adding to it
It is paid from savings, which then stop earning any interest at all
Its cost gets spread across many paychecks by automatic transfers
It forces investments to be sold, which locks in a large tax bill
questions.correctAnswer: It goes on a card or loan, where interest and fees keep adding to it
questions.explanation: Without a cushion, the emergency is borrowed, and interest and fees make it grow beyond the original bill. With a cushion, it becomes a withdrawal that you then rebuild.

source.quote: When an emergency goes on a card or a loan, the one-time expense can grow well beyond the original bill because of interest and fees. That is how one repair bill can keep costing long after it is paid.

questions.question: What problem can a scheduled transfer from checking to savings cause, and how does the chapter suggest guarding against it?
options: Missing an employer match; send the transfer to an IRA instead
Losing principal if the bank fails; move the money into mutual funds
Fees if checking is short that day; check the balance before it runs
Spending the cushion on wants; keep it in the everyday checking account
questions.correctAnswer: Fees if checking is short that day; check the balance before it runs
questions.explanation: An automatic transfer can trigger overdraft fees when checking can't cover it. The chapter says to watch the balance or set a reminder before the transfer runs.

source.quote: An automatic transfer can trigger overdraft fees if checking is short on the day it runs. Keep an eye on the balance, or set a reminder to check it before the transfer runs.

questions.question: How does keeping emergency money apart from investments help when the market falls?
options: It earns enough to outweigh the interest on high interest credit cards
It makes the invested money federally insured against loss of principal
A surprise bill need not be paid by selling investments that have dropped
It lets the investments take on more risk with no chance of any loss
questions.correctAnswer: A surprise bill need not be paid by selling investments that have dropped
questions.explanation: Investments can lose value, and the cushion means you don't have to sell them at a low point to cover a bill. The other options contradict the text: investments aren't insured, all carry risk, and no investment beats card interest for sure.

source.quote: This is the trade the cushion protects. With the emergency money held elsewhere, a bill need not be paid by selling investments after they have fallen.

questions.question: Fund A and Fund B hold the same investments, but Fund A costs 0.2% a year and Fund B costs 1.0% a year. Which should leave you with more money over time, and why?
options: Fund A, because lower yearly costs leave more of the returns
Fund B, because higher charges usually mean better management
Fund B, because managed funds generally charge lower fees
Neither, because small fee gaps even out over the years held
questions.correctAnswer: Fund A, because lower yearly costs leave more of the returns
questions.explanation: When two funds are alike except for their charges, the cheaper one leaves you more money. Small fees add up over the years.

source.quote: Of two funds alike in every way except their charges, the one with lower annual costs leaves you with more money.
